It explores how these innovations connect with the energy grid, the digital economy, artificial intelligence, and Internet of Things (IoT). With workforce gaps in building specializations on the rise, there is a growing need for skilled professionals from building science programs in undergraduate, graduate, or vocational settings to keep up with the demand (Law 2025). JUMP (Join the Discussion, Unveil Innovation, Make Connections, Promote Technology-to- Market) Into STEM is a U.S. collegiate building science competition that aims to inspire the next generation of building scientists by attracting student talent from disciplines like engineering, science, computer science, architecture, and others that might not be traditional pathways to a career in technology. It encourages innovative thinking and multidisciplinary collaboration to advance building technologies. The team-based competition directs participants to select a challenge and develop a comprehensive solution that addresses the problem statement, stakeholder needs, and technology-to-market barriers (Hubbard et al. 2021; Rippy et al. 2022). Submissions are then reviewed by a panel of judges representing the private sector, national laboratories, and academia. Lastly, winners from each challenge are invited to a final competition, where they refine their ideas and compete for a 10-week paid summer internship. To date, there have been seven annual cycles of JUMP Into STEM (2018–2025). The competition has engaged more than 1,200 student participants across 20 states. The program continues to inspire the upcoming generation of building scientists by presenting real-world challenge topics that are connected to contemporary problems and by promoting its aims and achievements through conference presentations and journal publications. This report presents a selection of key challenges from past competitions that are tailored for academic and industry professionals who aim to train or attract multidisciplinary talent to address current building science challenges. Additional considerations are included to facilitate effective replication of the challenge prompts. 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2 Challenges The problem statements or challenges developed for each competition period are designed to reflect issues critical to the building industry at that time, so the topics vary from year to year. Administered challenges over the last seven years of the competition can be grouped into four core themes: building envelopes, energy management, indoor environmental quality, and technology adoption.
